text:
A: Hiya! Oh, hello. Can you hear me?
B: Hello, love, yes, I can hear you. Sorry, I've just got my glasses on, hang on. There we go. I'm Julie.
A: Jago. Nice to meet you, Julie.
B: Jago, that's an unusual one, isn't it? Is that Cornish? Sorry, I saw the surf bits in your photo.
A: Yeah, spot on, it's Cornish. I'm in Truro. My nan picked it, basically. Where are you?
B: Basingstoke. Nothing exciting. Roundabouts, mostly.
A: [laughs] I've driven through it, I think. Loads of roundabouts, yeah. How's your day been?
B: Erm, alright. I was on an early, so I've been up since half five. I'm a care assistant at a care home. I'm absolutely shattered, to be honest, so if I start yawning it's not you.
A: No, fair play, that's proper hard work. My mum works at a GP surgery, she's the office manager, so she's always telling me what the care homes ring up about. Do you like it?
B: I do, yeah. I love the residents. It's the staffing that gets you, you know, when you're short and you've got twelve people to get up and dressed and their breakfasts, and the agency girl's on her phone. But the residents themselves, bless them, they're lovely. Some of them have got the best stories. One gentleman was in the war, and he still flirts with all of us.
A: See, that's what I love. I'm doing a film degree, and my final project's a documentary about gig rowing clubs, and the best bits are always the older lot. There's this fella, he's seventy-four, and he just sat in the boat shed and told me about rowing to the Scillies back in the eighties. I didn't have to ask him anything, I just pointed the camera.
B: Oh, that's lovely. That's what's missing, isn't it, people just listening to them.
A: Exactly that. You could probably make a better film than me, to be honest, you've got all the stories.
B: Oh, no, I wouldn't know where to start. I can barely get this laptop working. My son set it up.
A: How old's your son?
B: Liam's twenty-eight. He still lives with me, him and his girlfriend. He leaves his work boots right in the hallway, every single day. I've nearly gone flying three times this week.
A: [laughs] Oh, that's me. My mum would say exactly the same. I'm twenty-three and still at home, still having her roast every Sunday. I'm never moving out at this rate.
B: Well, why would you? A roast every Sunday, I'd stay. Does she do Yorkshires?
A: Massive ones. And she does the roast potatoes in goose fat, they're unreal.
B: Oh, she sounds like she knows what she's doing. I do mine in the oil, I can't stretch to goose fat with the price of a shop now.
A: To be fair, I think she only does it at Christmas, I'm embellishing. [laughs]
B: [laughs] I knew it! You've got that look. You remind me a bit of my Liam, actually, the hair. Sorry, is that a weird thing to say?
A: No, that's a compliment, I'll take it. Funnily enough, I said you looked like my mum on that photo bit.
B: Oh, bless you. Well, I hope she's—
